title: Securing AI Agents: Identity, Authorization, and the DPACT Framework
gist: An identity and access engineering leader argues that agents have already become delegated autonomous actors with real-world effects but without corresponding identity and authorization, and proposes DPACT (Delegation, Policy, Auditability, Context, Time) as the blueprint for bounding them. His central claim is that the number one failure mode in production agent systems today is missing identity infrastructure rather than model quality, and that the industry must move from giving an agent a key to issuing it a bounded task grant.

themes.theme: From chat windows to delegated actors

insights.claim: AI systems that began as low-stakes browser chat windows have moved into operations and now produce real-world effects without any corresponding identity and authorization layer, putting them in delegated autonomous actor territory rather than question-and-answer territory.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Frames agent identity as the missing infrastructure layer of the current AI buildout - the gap where new vendor categories form.
insights.quote: as agents moved into operations, they've started gaining real world effects without corresponding identity and authorization
insights.locator: The Shift to Agentic Systems Problem

insights.claim: The value of a software builder is shifting from raw individual coding skill to the ability to orchestrate agents, so the scarce skill becomes wielding agentic systems rather than writing lines of code.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A labour-mix thesis: headcount value migrates to orchestration roles, which changes what developer-tool buyers pay for.
insights.quote: the shift is evolving from can you write good code individually to, can you be that software orchestrator where you have agents accompanying you to help you build that?
insights.locator: The Shift to Agentic Systems Problem

insights.claim: Because agents run twenty four seven rather than during a human workday, the big AI and agent providers have moved software pricing from per seat to per token, and identity models must now mirror that metered, always-on consumption.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: The per-seat to per-token transition resets SaaS revenue models and the unit economics of every agent-heavy workflow.
insights.quote: they moved from a pay per seat to pay per token, given that now we're discussing about 24/7 availability
insights.locator: So what I hear you saying is the software as a service landscape is changing

insights.claim: Teams consistently race to agent capability and treat identity, accountability and trust as afterthoughts, when those are precisely the risky components; the safer design order is delegation first, with scopes, grants and policies defined before the agent has power.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A diligence question for any company deploying agents: was delegation designed before capability, or bolted on after?
insights.locator: But one of the real problem where I see it

insights.claim: The DPACT framework defines five must-haves for guardrailing an agent: Delegation (on whose behalf it acts), Policy (what it may and explicitly may not do), Auditability (why it took an action, reviewable months later), Context (the boundary it operates within) and Time (when its authority ends).
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A checklist an investor or buyer can run against any agentic product to score whether its guardrails are real.
insights.quote: it stands for delegation, policy, auditability, context and time
insights.locator: Acting on Behalf of vs. Impersonating

insights.claim: Granting an agent read access to a database table without a time bound confers perpetual authority, so explicit expiry through TTLs or task-scoped grants is required to end an agent's authority.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Long-lived grants are the agentic equivalent of standing credentials - a specific, auditable control gap to look for.
insights.locator: And time is when does authority end?

insights.claim: Agent audit logs serve a dual purpose: they answer why an action was taken, and they become the input to a feedback loop that retrains the agent to make better decisions.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Audit data becomes a training asset, which raises the strategic value of owning the agent observability layer.
insights.locator: Auditability or explainability is today, 30 days later

insights.claim: The context boundary is best expressed as explicit prohibitions rather than permissions, of the form draft an email but do not send it.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Negative-space policy definition is the practical implementation detail that distinguishes working guardrails from aspirational ones.
insights.quote: Draft an email, but don't send it. That is the context.
insights.locator: And see context. What is this boundary

insights.claim: DPACT is currently a positional blueprint with no tooling or implementation attached, deliberately leaving delegation models and policy engines to be implemented per stack.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: The governance layer for agents is still conceptual, which means the implementation market is unclaimed.
insights.quote: It's a blueprint. It's a positional framework that can be applied in several different ways.
insights.locator: We are calling it the framework

insights.claim: The same guardrail framework is meant to serve three buyer cohorts simultaneously: engineers implementing controls, product managers judging production readiness, and executives assessing whether the agent estate is betting the company.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Multi-cohort framing is how governance tooling gets budget above the engineering line item.
insights.locator: And in combination of this becomes a framework

insights.claim: The core security principle for agents is that they should always act on behalf of a named human user and never impersonate that user, because impersonation is where policy and security violations originate and where over-privilege creeps in.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: On-behalf-of versus impersonation is the single cleanest technical test for whether an agent deployment is safe.
insights.quote: agents should always act on behalf of a human user and should never ever impersonate a user
insights.locator: Acting on Behalf of vs. Impersonating

insights.claim: The first release of the tool now known as OpenClaw is cited as a case study in which agent delegation failures produced a security nightmare before being fixed.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Public post-mortems of early agent tools are the cheapest available training data on where agent security breaks.
insights.locator: we famously know the tool as OpenClaw today

insights.claim: Agent permissioning has two failure poles: over-privileged agents that can do anything asked of them and are dangerous, and over-restricted agents that are worthless because they constantly nag humans for permission.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Explains why blunt approval gates fail commercially - the governance product that wins must preserve autonomy while bounding it.
insights.quote: One is a very over-privileged agent, which is dangerous and pretty much can do anything that you ask it to do, an over-restricted agent, which pretty much means these agents are worthless.
insights.locator: In fact, I should correct myself

insights.claim: The pre-AI identity model in which humans access apps and apps access resources with a human always in the loop fundamentally breaks for agents that decide autonomously and chain calls to other tools, so decades of human-centric access control cannot be mapped one-to-one onto agents.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: If existing IAM primitives genuinely do not transfer, incumbents must rebuild rather than extend - a rare opening for challengers.
insights.locator: One of the good ways to think about this agent tech ecosystem

insights.claim: As frontier models improve, the autonomy and intent of the agent built on them changes underneath the infrastructure, so identity assumptions that hold today can be invalidated by the next model release.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Model upgrades are a live risk to deployed security assumptions - a recurring operational cost few buyers have priced.
insights.locator: They can chain and call other tools

themes.theme: Real incidents and the cost of unbounded scope

insights.claim: A company using a semi-agentic chat interface for hiring interviews saw its token and agentic infrastructure bills go haywire after applicants prompt-injected the interview bot into writing Python scripts for fun, and had to shut the agent capability down.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Missing context boundaries show up first as an uncontrolled cloud bill, making token spend an early warning indicator of agent misconfiguration.
insights.quote: their token builds and agentic info builds started to go haywire
insights.locator: Maybe take an example from a case study

insights.claim: The same abuse pattern recurred with a food-ordering agentic chatbot asked to tell jokes and write Python, making unbounded scope a direct and recurring operating expense rather than a theoretical risk.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: End-user abuse of consumer-facing agents is a predictable cost line - watch gross margin at companies deploying open-ended chat agents.
insights.quote: It's completely your responsibility to define what the agent can do and most important to what it cannot do.
insights.locator: Several similar incidents were noticed

insights.claim: A customer service agent handling a genuine double-charge refund can, without guardrails, pattern-match the same incident across ten other customers, issue all of them refunds and email them a 60% discount coupon, converting one correct decision into mass unauthorised liability.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Quantifies how agent generalisation turns a single correct action into uncontrolled financial exposure - a real P&L risk in customer operations.
insights.quote: the agent with improper guardrails can also pull up similar incident for 10 other customers and start issuing all of them refunds
insights.locator: Mapping DPACT to Product Decisions

insights.claim: The dominant failure mode in production agent systems today is not model quality but the absence of identity systems, a view that runs against the industry's focus on model and prompt quality.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: If correct, spend shifts from model upgrades to identity and authorization infrastructure - a different set of winners.
insights.quote: the number one failure mode today in the production systems is not just purely because of the model quality, it's also because of the lack of identity systems
insights.locator: So the preliminary thing is a lot of the things

insights.claim: Agent systems built on recent frontier models such as Claude Mythos and Fable 5 can not only operate within a system but work out what they can do and break it, so infrastructure-level guardrails rather than model-level trust are the control point.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Capability growth is adversarial to existing containment - security spend scales with model capability, not inversely.
insights.locator: And this was proven by some of the most recent frontier models

insights.claim: The first governance step for an organisation with agents already in production is an inventory: which agents exist, what tools they can call, what credentials they use, what data they can access, and who owns them.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Inventory-first is the same playbook that created the CSPM and CMDB markets - expect an agent-inventory product category.
insights.locator: Incremental Adoption of Agent Governance

insights.claim: After inventory, the next steps are adding agent IDs, task IDs and trace IDs for basic visibility, then separating agent identity from human identity instead of passing human tokens or API keys into agents where they can leak.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A concrete maturity ladder for assessing how far along any enterprise agent programme actually is.
insights.locator: Once you can have achieved that second step

insights.claim: The end state of the ladder is continuous authorization, where policy is evaluated at every step and access is downgraded or revoked when an agent's scope increases or it moves toward a dangerous area.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Continuous authorization extends Zero Trust to machine actors and is the likely shape of the next enterprise security budget line.
insights.locator: and then move forward towards continuous authorization

insights.claim: The highest-risk factors to remove first are bottled human tokens, long-lived keys, broad service accounts attached to agent services, missing auditing, missing revocation strategy and missing task boundaries.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A six-item risk checklist that makes agent security posture quickly auditable from the outside.
insights.locator: And to avoid making the whole governance a giant upfront program

insights.claim: The first maturity milestone in agent governance is not a perfect policy but simply knowing which agents can act and what authority they currently hold.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Sets a low, achievable bar that most organisations still fail - which is itself the size of the market opportunity.
insights.quote: the first maturity step is not a perfect policy. It is knowing which agents can act and what authority they can currently have
insights.locator: And in my experience, the first maturity step

themes.theme: What agent infrastructure vendors must ship

insights.claim: Identity and access management providers should make agent on-behalf-of grants a first-class out-of-the-box feature: a short-lived second layer of token derived from a human identity, valid only in the agent's context, from which nothing can be concluded back to the user or reused maliciously.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: A specific, testable product requirement for judging whether an IAM vendor is genuinely agent-ready or repackaging service accounts.
insights.quote: An IAM provider should support first class, and first class is the key word here, agent on behalf of grants.
insights.locator: The Future of IAM Vendors and Agent Infrastructure

insights.claim: Tool providers should validate grants and emit structured audit events, because without a proper audit channel the only available answer to why an agent acted is that it is AI and it just did it, which destroys customer trust.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Auditability becomes a commercial requirement, not a compliance nicety - unexplainable agents lose enterprise deals.
insights.locator: I also think that the tool provider should validate grants

insights.claim: The next platform perimeter should be delegated agent authority rather than another surface for pasting a long-lived API key, with agent frameworks exposing task and agent identity, tool-call traces, review hooks and policy integration points.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Names the next security perimeter explicitly - the layer where the next generation of infrastructure vendors will compete.
insights.quote: the next platform perimeter should be delegated agent authority, not another place to just paste a long lived API key
insights.locator: So to close this out

insights.claim: The industry is currently between issuing an agent a key and issuing it a semi-bounded task grant, and legacy systems built for human identity will face the hardest and most expensive migration to fully bounded grants.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Legacy identity estates are the friction point - migration cost is revenue for whoever supplies the bridge.
insights.quote: the ecosystem collectively needs to move from saying give the agent a key to issue the agent a bounded task grant
insights.locator: That is more or less the perspective

insights.claim: Bounded agent authority already has an everyday precedent: a babysitter is hired for fixed hours, allowed to spend a capped amount on food, given a bedtime rule and no access to bank accounts, Social Security numbers or house keys, and their authority ends when the parents return.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: An intuitive mental model executives can act on, which makes the governance sale far easier than abstract policy language.
insights.quote: why are we handing over full authority to our agents when we are building that for the industry, for the tasks that we are doing?
insights.locator: Everybody who's building, using the agents

insights.claim: The boundary between a real human and an agent acting on a human's behalf will keep blurring, and it is already difficult to tell which is responding at the other end of an interaction.
insights.speaker: Sahil Agarwal
insights.so_what: Verification of human versus agent identity becomes its own product requirement across communications, commerce and support.
insights.quote: the barrier or the line between a real human and an agent acting on behalf of human is going to get blurry and blurry
insights.locator: And the only thing that I'd say
